In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the OGTT is not recommended as a screening test in asymptomatic children and adolescents.
the 1h‐GL ≥8.6 mmol/L during an OGTT in children and adolescents identifies an increased risk for type 2 diabetes mellitus, and an unfavouriable cardiometabolic and inflammation profile.
the 1h‐GL ≥8.6mmol/L is a useful tool for the identification of children with abnormal glucose metabolism, but it should not be considered an isolated criterion for the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
elevated 1‐hour plasma glucose identifies obese children with abnormal glucose metabolism, and an unfavourably altered inflammatory profile.
elevated 1h-OGTT is associated with a pro-inflammatory state, and that this state is associated with the presence of insulin resistance.
the elevated 1h‐PLG in obese children identifies a subgroup of children with abnormal glucose metabolism, increased insulin resistance and increased adiposity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 1h‐GL ≥8.6mmol/L cut‐off is a useful tool to identify obese children and adolescents at high risk for type 1 and type 2 diabetes and for metabolic syndrome.
elevated plasma glucose levels at 1h‐GL are associated with a higher risk for developing diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.
1‐h‐GL ≥8.6mmol/L in obese children and youth identifies those with abnormal glucose metabolism.
